# Calibration Board Studio

[简体中文](README.zh-CN.md) · English

A browser-only editor for designing and exporting calibration targets. Every page, pattern, and layout value is stored in millimeters, and generation, layout, and export all run locally — there is no backend service.

Live site: <https://calib.qvleka.cn>. This repository contains the source and deployment instructions.

**Development note:** The vast majority of the source code in this repository was generated by AI. The project is maintained as open-source software.

Contents: [Get started](#get-started) · [Deployment URL](#deployment-url) · [Targets](#targets) · [Workflow](#workflow) · [Snapping](#canvas-sketch-style-snapping) · [Dimensions](#dimensions) · [Controls](#keyboard-and-mouse) · [Coordinates](#coordinates-and-detector-conventions) · [Export](#export-and-print-accuracy) · [Projects](#projects-and-local-data) · [Language](#interface-language) · [Source map](#source-map)

## Get started

Requirements: Node.js 22 or newer and npm.

```bash
npm ci
npm run dev      # development server
npm run build    # type check + production build into dist/
npm run preview  # serve the production build locally
```

## Deployment URL

The default `npm run build` is ready to deploy at a domain root or subdirectory: its asset paths are relative and there is no domain to edit. If you want an absolute canonical URL and a sitemap for search engines, set `SITE_URL` to **your own public URL** at build time, including its path if hosted in a subdirectory:

```bash
SITE_URL=https://example.com/calibration/ npm run build
```

With `SITE_URL`, the build uses that URL for asset paths, the canonical link, the Open Graph URL, and `dist/sitemap.xml`. For a site at the domain root, `dist/robots.txt` also points to the sitemap. For a subdirectory deployment, submit the sitemap directly to the search engine: crawlers only read `robots.txt` at the domain root. Without `SITE_URL`, the build has no canonical URL or sitemap and keeps a generic `robots.txt` that allows crawling. Publish the contents of `dist/` at your deployment URL; a sitemap only helps discovery after it is publicly available.

## Targets

| Target | Options | Default size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chessboard | Columns, rows, square size, first square color | 105 × 150 mm (7×10 × 15 mm) |
| Circle grid | Columns, rows, pitch, diameter | 97 × 142 mm (7×10, pitch 15 mm) |
| Asymmetric circles | Columns, rows, pitch, diameter | 90 × 126 mm (4×11, pitch 12 mm) |
| ArUco | Single marker, GridBoard; 4×4, 5×5, 6×6, 7×7 dictionaries; starting ID | 80 × 80 mm / 92 × 140 mm |
| ChArUco | Squares, marker size, dictionary, first square, marker ID starting corner and starting ID | 105 × 150 mm (7×10, 15 mm squares) |
| AprilTag | Single tag, regular grid; 16h5, 25h9, 36h10, 36h11 families; starting ID | 80 × 80 mm / 95 × 120 mm |
| AprilGrid | Symmetric corner pattern, tag size, spacing ratio, family, starting corner and ID | 113.4 × 113.4 mm (6×6 tags) |
| Custom binary | Editable matrix of 0 and 1 cells with a physical cell size | 80 × 70 mm |

The default targets fit a landscape A4 sheet together with their annotations. Marker codewords are bundled in `src/data/markers.json`.

## Workflow

1. **Project and paper.** Pick a paper preset (A0–A6, Letter, Legal, Tabloid) or a custom size, in portrait or landscape orientation. There is no size ceiling: a 20 mm marker page and a several-metre floor target both work, and a side beyond 10 000 mm is flagged rather than blocked, because ordinary printing and PDF (200 in / 5080 mm per side) stop applying there. The project name is suggested and can be edited later. While nothing is selected the inspector shows the page settings; clicking empty paper brings them back at any time.
2. **Target.** Choose a pattern and enter its physical parameters. Geometry is protected: change the parameters instead of stretching the layer. Single markers pin their coordinate frame with the **Z axis** option, and ChArUco exposes its first square (see [coordinates](#coordinates-and-detector-conventions)).
3. **Layers.** Add text, a rectangle, a circle, a line, a 100 mm print check line, or a PNG/JPEG image. Click to select and drag to move. Names are editable — double-click a name in the layer list, use the pencil that appears on hover, or edit **Layer name** in the inspector; a duplicate name gets a number appended automatically. Each board folds with its caret, and **Collapse all** folds or unfolds every board.
4. **Child layers.** Every board carries **XY axes** and a **parameter label**; targets with coded markers add an **ID labels** layer that numbers each marker. It starts hidden — enable it from the layer list when you want to check or document IDs. Show, hide, move, scale, and (optionally) rotate them independently.
5. **Dimensions.** See [Dimensions](#dimensions) below.
6. **Layout.** The **Layout** tab has two sub-menus: **Drawing dimensions** opens first, **Alignment tools** holds page/margin/edge-to-edge alignment. Opening Alignment tools turns off the dimension tool, so the canvas is ready to select and move layers.
7. **Export.** PDF, SVG, PNG (150/300/600 DPI), or a JSON project. Dimension lines and print-scale compensation are optional, and a check line added under **Layers** travels with the drawing.

## Canvas: sketch-style snapping

Dragging a layer infers relations the way a CAD sketch does, so layers land where they belong without typing coordinates:

- **Alignment** — edge, center, and edge-to-edge contact with any visible layer, plus the paper edges and the paper center. The inferred line is drawn while you drag.
- **Equal spacing** — the layer is centred between two neighbours with equal gaps, or continues an existing gap rhythm. Both gaps are labelled with the same value.
- **Grid** — 1 mm by default, switchable to 0.5, 2, 5 mm or off. It catches positions no relation covers; an inferred relation always wins over the grid.
- **Live readout** — the status bar shows the position, the four paper margins, the active relation, and a warning when the layer leaves the page.

Snapping only writes position values into the document; exported geometry is unaffected.

## Dimensions

Dimension lines belong to the **Layout** tab, and switching to it arms the dimension tool automatically — a banner announces that and retires on the first canvas click (or after a few seconds). Press **Esc**, the banner button, or the ruler button to get the normal pointer back for moving layers. Other tabs show a chip that jumps to Layout when the project already has dimensions.

**Creating.** Click two edges along the same axis: layer borders, layer centre lines, and the paper border are all pickable. The first click sets the reference and the second the measured object; dragging right after the second click pulls the line out to the distance you want. Continue clicking to create more.

**Editing.** A single click on a line selects it and opens the inspector (the selection survives releasing the mouse; on narrow screens the inspector slides in):

- **Measured value** — the sign says which side the measured edge sits on: positive is right or below the reference, negative is left or above, so the same number distinguishes the two cases and a negative value moves the object across. **Flip to the other side** does the same in one click, and **0** aligns the two edges.
- **Joint solving** — other dimensions measure the same geometry, so the editor looks for an arrangement that satisfies the edit *and* keeps them intact: layers tied together by an existing dimension move as a group (a label dimensioned to the board travels with the board), and a dimension inside one shape resizes it and shifts it so the edges other dimensions read stay in place. When a joint solution exists it is applied silently, with a note that several layers moved.
- **Conflicts** — when no arrangement exists, the edit is held back and listed: the conflicting dimensions, their current values, and what they would become. Choose **Change anyway** (move only the measured object, accepting the knock-on effects) or **Cancel**.
- **Measurement only** — a dimension that spans a single board or text layer reports a value but cannot drive it; rectangles, circles, lines, and images resize.
- **Line position and ink** — type the offset from the geometry or drag the line (negative offsets put it on the other side). Set the color for each dimension, including its line, arrows, leaders, and value. Thickness and value font size default to 0.5 mm and 5 mm.
- **Drawing style** — the measured line carries a filled arrowhead at each end (they flip to the outside when the span is too short for two arrows, which keeps the value readable), and the two leader lines show where the dimension is anchored. Both are pickable per dimension: arrows as **filled**, **open**, **architectural tick**, **dot**, or none, and leaders as **automatic**, **dashed**, **thin solid**, **short stubs only**, or hidden.
- **Leaders that stay out of the way** — a leader always starts on the side of the object that faces the dimension line, so pulling a dimension above or to the left of a layer no longer draws a line through it. The automatic style keeps the dashed leader while it is short and breaks it into a stub at each end once it would run further than 30 mm, which is what happens when two far-apart edges are measured against each other.
- **Objects** — switch the measured object, the reference (paper or another layer), and both edges.
- **Visibility and deletion** — from the same panel, or from the list in the Layout tab, which shows every dimension with its signed value.

While the tool is armed, existing lines can still be selected, double-clicked to edit their value, or dragged to adjust their position. Dimensions are stored in the project and drawn only while the Layout tab is open. The export dialog decides whether exported files include them.

## Keyboard and mouse

| Input | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Click / drag | Select a layer; drag to move it (with snapping) |
| Double-click a layer name | Rename it |
| Double-click a dimension line | Type its value in place |
| Arrow keys | Nudge the selection by 0.1 mm |
| Shift + arrows | Nudge by 1 mm |
| Shift while dragging | Lock the drag to one axis |
| Alt while dragging | Suspend snapping for that move |
| Esc | Leave the dimension tool, then clear the selection |
| Delete / Backspace | Delete the selected dimension |
| Ctrl/Cmd + Z, Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Z | Undo, redo |
| Enter / Esc in a field | Commit / cancel the edit |
| Drag a panel divider, double-click it | Resize a side panel, or restore its default width |
| Arrow keys on a focused divider | Nudge that panel by 16 px |

The magnet button in the canvas toolbar toggles smart snapping and the neighbouring menu selects the grid step.
When the board has validation issues, click the count in the center of the bottom status bar to read every reason.

The workspace chooses its layout from the available width and interface scale: wide windows show both panels, medium windows keep the tools docked and open properties on demand, and phones give the canvas the remaining height with separate tool and property drawers. At the default font size, the breakpoints are 1180 and 760 CSS pixels; they grow with the interface scale. Shrinking a window preserves saved panel widths. New, import, save, and export remain available on narrow screens, and dialogs scroll within short windows.

The **interface scale** menu offers auto and 100%, 110%, 125%, 150%, 175%, or 200%. It changes text and controls while preserving physical board dimensions. The canvas starts in **fit to window** mode and responds to window, panel, and paper size changes. Manual zoom or resetting to 100% preserves the chosen zoom until you press fit again. Enlarged pages remain scrollable all the way to their top and left edges.
The color picker beside the scale menu changes the interface accent and remembers it in this browser. **Restore default settings** resets the accent, interface scale, panel widths, browser language preference, snapping and grid step, and returns the canvas to fit-to-window zoom. The current project and its geometry stay intact.

## Coordinates and detector conventions

Page coordinates start at the top-left and increase rightward and downward. Geometry is always generated from parameters, never from preview pixels or screen zoom.

**Axes mark.** The XY mark is anchored to the board's origin corner, just outside the pattern on the extension of its diagonal, so the arrows point into the pattern without covering it. Changing the origin corner or rotating a printed target changes how a detector interprets the layout: configure the detector with the same layout and ID order.

**Grid targets** place the origin at an arrangement corner, so the origin control applies to them. A **single marker** has no arrangement: the origin is the marker center and the frame is pinned by the **Z axis** option instead.

| Z axis | Frame | Axes drawn at | Default for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Out of the marker | X right, Y up, Z out | Bottom-left corner | ArUco single marker (OpenCV's marker frame) |
| Into the marker | X right, Y down, Z in | Top-left corner | AprilTag single marker (the AprilTag library's frame for the officially oriented tag) |

Both frames are right-handed and differ by a 180° rotation about X, so pick the one your detector reports.

**ChArUco** starts with an ArUco marker in the top-left square. That is the arrangement OpenCV produced before 4.6 and restores with `setLegacyPattern(true)` on a board with an even row count; OpenCV 4.6 and newer default to a black first square, which is available as **black chess square**. The printed board and the detector definition must agree, including the marker ID sequence when the starting ID changes.

**AprilGrid** defaults to a bottom-left origin and starting ID 0, with IDs increasing left to right and then upward, two black border bits per tag, and symmetric black squares at gap intersections. The standard Kalibr implementation uses tag36h11 and maps detected IDs directly to grid positions, so a nonzero starting ID, another family, or another starting corner needs detector support. See the [Kalibr source](https://github.com/ethz-asl/kalibr/blob/master/aslam_cv/aslam_cameras_april/src/GridCalibrationTargetAprilgrid.cpp).

## Export and print accuracy

PDF and SVG keep vector geometry and a page size expressed in millimeters; PNG is rasterized at the selected DPI. Print at **100% / actual size** with "fit to page" disabled. Add a 100 mm check line under **Layers** (it is exactly 100 mm long and cannot be resized — moving, recolouring, and re-weighting it are the only edits), print it, measure it, and enter the measured length for compensation; check that the compensated design still fits the page and your printer's printable area.

Non-ASCII text is embedded as an image in PDF output; markers and geometric primitives stay vector. Large PNG exports are limited by browser memory, with a 120 million pixel safeguard. A PDF page cannot exceed 200 in / 5080 mm per side, so an oversized page is offered as SVG or PNG instead; those two formats have no such limit.

## Projects and local data

The current project is saved automatically in this browser's local storage. Export JSON for a portable copy; import accepts files that match the current schema. No migration is provided, and `version` guards it:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "name": "calibration-board-01",
  "width": 210,
  "height": 297,
  "layers": [],
  "dimensions": []
}
```

- Board layers need `pluginId`, `params`, and all three child entries `children.axes`, `children.info`, and `children.ids`. Each child carries `visible`, `offsetX`, `offsetY`, and optionally `title` (custom name), `scale`, `rotation`.
- A board also stores the layer-tree `collapsed` flag; marker-ID targets expose `markers(params)` for the ID overlay.
- Dimensions carry `targetId`/`targetEdge`, `referenceId`/`referenceEdge`, `offset`, `visible`, and optionally `lineWidth`, `fontSize`, and `color`. Values are signed: positive means the measured edge is right of or below the reference.
- Types live in `src/core/model.ts`, import validation in `src/core/project.ts`. All lengths are millimeters.

No project data is sent to a server by the app.

## Interface language

The interface is available in Chinese and English. The masthead switch shows both options. On a first visit it follows the browser's preferred languages — Chinese for a `zh*` preference, English for `en*`, English otherwise — and your choice is remembered once you use the switch.
